intro: To call the doctor at night with an SBAR script, speak four parts in order: Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. Then ask for a specific action and read back every order you receive. This guide gives you the script, the checks to run before you dial, and the steps if nobody calls back.
tldr: Open with who you are, which patient, and the one problem, in one or two sentences.
Give the background, your assessment, and a specific request the provider can say yes or no to.
Get read-back on every order, then write down the time, the name, and what was decided.
If no one answers or helps, use the escalation path on your card, not your memory.

blocks.text: Night calls are where a clear script matters most. The provider may be asleep or covering several units. You have one patient in front of you, and the clock is running. SBAR gives you a fixed order to speak in, so you do not have to build the call from memory while your heart is racing. This page covers the script, the checks before you dial, what to do when nobody calls back, and what Lazur can and cannot do for you.
The SBAR script, line by line

SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. Each letter is one part of the call, spoken in that order. Situation tells the provider who you are, where the patient is, and what is happening now. Background gives the few facts that explain why. Assessment is your clinical read on the problem. Recommendation is the specific thing you want the provider to do.

items: Situation: I'm [your name], the RN on [unit], calling about [patient name] in room [room]. I'm worried about [problem] right now.
Background: Admitted for [reason]. Post-op [day] or other key history. Allergies are [allergies]. Code status is [status]. Current orders include [key orders].
Assessment: The last vital signs were [values] at [time], and the trend is [up, down or flat]. I think this patient is [your read].
Recommendation: I need you to [specific action], or tell me what you want me to do until you arrive. Can you read back the orders I have?

blocks.text: The brackets are where your facts go. Keep each slot short. A long call at night makes the provider work harder to find the one thing that matters. Give the numbers, not your feeling about them. 'Pressure is falling' is useful. 'I don't like how she looks' is not useful on its own, though your read still belongs in the call.

blocks.title: Ask for something specific
blocks.text: Your recommendation should be an action the provider can accept or refuse. 'Please come see the patient' works. 'What should we do?' makes the provider start from zero, and that costs time you may not have.

Here is a worked example of the whole call. It is a made-up case for teaching, not a protocol. Your unit's standards come first. Dr. Lee, this is [your name], the RN on the surgical floor, calling about the patient in room [room]. I'm worried about breathing and blood pressure. The patient had hip surgery yesterday and has a penicillin allergy. Blood pressure and heart rate have both moved the wrong way since the last check. I'm not sure what's causing it. I need you to come see the patient, or tell me what you want before you arrive. Can you read back the orders I have?

Notice what is missing. There is no tour of the chart, no apology for calling, and no guess about what the provider will say. The caller names the problem early, gives the trend, and asks for something. If you have your facts ready, the call stays short. Short is the goal, because the provider can decide faster.
What to gather before you dial

Many bad night calls go wrong because the nurse started dialing before knowing the answers. Spend a minute on the chart first. Pull up the last vital signs and check when they were taken. Look at what you have already done, including medicines given and the times you gave them. Confirm the code status and allergies. Write these on a sticky note or on your card, where you can see them while you talk.

items: Vital signs with times, and whether the trend is up, down or flat.
Medicines given since the last call, with the times you gave them.
Allergies, code status, and any active orders that affect this problem.
Your assessment in one sentence, written down before you call.
The exact action you want, so your recommendation is ready to say.
Whether a charge nurse or colleague has seen the patient too.

blocks.text: The one-sentence assessment is the step people skip. Writing it forces you to choose a read. 'I think this is a fluid problem, and I'm not sure' is a real assessment. It tells the provider where you stand, and that helps them decide how fast to move. An honest 'I'm not sure' is more useful than a confident guess you cannot support.
Get a second read before the call

If a colleague or charge nurse can look at the patient with you, do that before you call. A second look takes a few minutes. It can turn a vague worry into a clear one, or show you that the trend is already known. If the patient is getting worse fast, do not wait for a huddle. Call now, and bring the colleague in as you go.
What to do when the provider does not call back

An unanswered call is a common night problem, and your unit probably has a written answer for it. That answer is your escalation path. It is the list of people to contact, in order, when the first call fails. Depending on your facility, the chain may run from the provider to the charge nurse, then to a supervisor or a rapid response contact. Check your own unit's version, not someone else's.

The research found a specific gap here. In a study at one 691-bed academic center in the Northeastern US, staff were unclear about contacts beyond the provider and the immediate supervisor. The full matrix with phone numbers was held by nursing managers. The posted copies left the numbers off. If your posted copy has no numbers, the gap is not your fault, but it is yours to close.
Why nurses hesitate to call at night

The clearest number comes from a 2023 to 2024 survey at one academic medical center. Of the 89 respondents who had faced a safety concern, 48 hesitated to act. They were not sure how to escalate. That is 53.9% of that group. The response rate was about 9%, so treat the result as a clue about the problem, not a measure of how common it is across hospitals.

Another 47% of respondents said they were still unsure how to use the escalation matrix. Another 41% were ambivalent about whether the pathway had made them more confident. Two respondents named fear of retaliation as a reason to hold back. That count is small. Still, it appears in nurses' own words, so it belongs in the conversation on your unit.

blocks.text: The SBAR evidence points the same way, with limits. A 2026 systematic review covered 15 English-language open-access studies published from 2019 to 2024. It says structured SBAR-type handover tools 'may support improvements in communication quality and patient safety.' Certainty is low to moderate. The time effects are mixed. One study found SBAR time-consuming, and another found no significant change in total handover time, although the median fell by about 61 seconds.
What staying quiet costs the patient and the team

A late or vague call costs the patient time, because the provider has to ask questions before deciding. The team pays too. The NCSBN 2024 National Nursing Workforce Study reports 39.9% of RNs intend to leave the workforce or retire within five years. Among nurses planning to leave, excluding retirement, about 41.5% named stress and burnout as the root cause. Those figures are not a verdict on any one unit. They do show why small fixes to nights are worth the effort.

blocks.title: What the numbers cannot tell you
blocks.text: The 41.5% figure covers nurses planning to leave, not all nurses. The NCSBN release does not split it by RN and LPN/VN. Use it as context for workforce stress, not as a rate for your own hospital.
Fixes you can use tonight, for free

None of these fixes needs a purchase. They need a printer, a pen, and one conversation with your manager. Start with the card, because it helps on the next call. The other fixes make the card more useful over time.

items: Make a one-page SBAR card. In Word, choose Insert > Table, add four rows, and label them S, B, A and R. Add lines for read-back, the call time and the name of the person you reached.
Ask your manager for the full escalation matrix with phone numbers. Compare it with the posted copy. Write any missing numbers on your card in pencil.
Write the chain of command on the card in the order your policy gives. If the order is unclear, ask your manager to confirm it in writing.
Say the call aloud on a quiet shift. Read the card once for each part. Change any line that sounds like an apology or a question.
Ask for read-back on every order. Write the order, the time and the name of the person who gave it. Repeat it back before you hang up.
Set a callback check in Apple Reminders. When the check fires, use the next contact on the chain if no one has returned the call.
If work alerts reach your Mac, open System Settings > Focus, select your Focus, click Allowed Apps, and turn on Time Sensitive Notifications. Then check Notifications settings for that app.

blocks.text: Practice matters more than polish. A card you have read aloud twice is more useful than a perfect card you have never used. Keep the card at the station, where you will see it before the phone rings, not in a folder in the back office.
Where Lazur helps, and where it stops

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. For this problem, that is the most useful part. You can ask where the on-call number sits on a policy PDF you already have open.

Lazur does not dial the provider, click buttons, or type into the chart. It does not run the call or make a clinical decision. It is not a plugin for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. Treat it as a second pair of eyes on your screen and a fast way to find things. You still make the call.

items: Point: find the escalation number or policy line on a page you have open.
Explain: read the text on screen out loud, then check the summary against the written policy.
Dictate: hold fn and speak your own notes into a blank document, at the cursor.
Everyday: set a timer or a Reminders item for a callback check, with no patient details in it.
Guide: ask Lazur to walk you through a setting one click at a time, waiting for each click.

blocks.title: Patient data and your employer's rules
blocks.text: When you hold ⌥⌘, Lazur sends the audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Even so, keep patient names and identifiers off screen unless your employer's policy allows it. Follow your employer's rules for patient data first.

A simple habit helps. Close the chart, or move it off screen, before you hold the shortcut. Ask about the policy PDF or a blank card instead. Keep identifiers out of anything Lazur touches, and paste text into the chart only the way your policy allows.

For notes, dictation is the more practical feature. Open a blank Word document, place the cursor where the text should go, and hold fn. Speak the SBAR lines in your own words, without identifiers, and check every word before you save. Lazur does not know your patient's chart, so the record is only as good as your review. More on this is in [how to dictate nursing notes on Mac without Dragon](/for/nurses/problems/dictate-nursing-notes-mac-without-dragon).
Mistakes that make night calls go wrong

items: Starting with the history instead of the problem. The provider needs the situation first.
Describing how you feel without the numbers behind it.
Recommending nothing, then waiting for the provider to decide your next step.
Skipping read-back, so an order is heard wrong or only half heard.
Calling once, hearing no answer, and stopping. Use the chain of command.
Skipping the note. A call with no time and no response on record is hard to follow later.
Working from an escalation list in memory. Numbers change, so check the current copy.

blocks.text: The last mistake is the quiet one. Nurses sometimes wait because they think the problem will pass, or because the provider was short with them last time. Your assessment is still valid. A call that turns out to be unneeded is a small cost. A call you skip can be hard to explain later, to the provider, to your manager, or to yourself.
Document the call before the shift ends

Write the time you called, who you spoke with, what you said in one line, what they ordered or decided, and the read-back. Keep the note factual and short. If the call relates to an event that went wrong, the guidance on [writing an objective nurse incident report](/for/nurses/problems/nurse-incident-report-objective-wording) covers how to word it. Check your facility's form and where your notes belong.
What the evidence does and does not show

Be honest about what is known. SBAR-type tools have a 2026 systematic review behind them, but certainty is low to moderate and the time effects are mixed. The escalation matrix study comes from one academic center, with a response rate near 9%. It found the gap in contacts and numbers. It did not test a fix, and the research behind this page did not turn up an outcome evaluation of a printed escalation pathway.

So the fixes here are reasonable steps, not proven cures. Test them on your own unit. If a fix makes calls clearer, keep it. If it adds noise, drop it, and bring the result to your manager or practice council. Your own observations from a few real calls are worth writing down.

blocks.title: A good test of any fix
blocks.text: Ask one question after each night shift. Did the card make the call shorter, clearer, or easier to start? If the answer is no, change the card rather than the nurse.
Where to go next

Start with the card, and print it before your next shift. If you keep your notes in Word, the [Word guide for nurses](/for/nurses/word) covers handoff sheets and SBAR forms. Policy pages you read in a browser are covered in the [Chrome guide for nurses](/for/nurses/chrome). Lazur's plans and trial are on the [pricing page](/pricing), and the app is on the [download page](/download).

faq.question: Is there one official SBAR script for calling a doctor at night?
faq.answer: No single wording is official. SBAR is the order you speak in: Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. Your hospital may have a standard card or preferred phrases. If it does, use that, and treat the wording in this guide as a starting point.

faq.question: What if the provider does not call back?
faq.answer: Call the next contact on your unit's escalation path, and note each attempt with the time. The path may name the charge nurse, a supervisor or a rapid response contact, depending on your facility. Check the written policy rather than relying on memory.

faq.question: Should I say 'I'm worried' or 'I'm concerned' on the call?
faq.answer: Say what you see first, then what worries you. 'I'm worried' gives the provider a feeling to weigh. A trend, a specific finding and a clear request give them something they can act on.

faq.question: Does Lazur call the doctor or dial for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not dial, click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can point to the number on your screen, read text out loud and help you dictate notes. You still make the call.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with a patient chart open?
faq.answer: Be careful. Holding ⌥⌘ sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. Do not hold the shortcut with patient identifiers on screen unless your employer allows it, and follow your employer's rules for patient data.

faq.question: Where do I find the full escalation matrix with phone numbers?
faq.answer: Ask your nurse manager. In the study behind this page, the full matrix with phone numbers was held by nursing managers, while posted copies left the numbers off. Ask for a copy you can keep at the station.

faq.question: Does dictation replace writing up the call?
faq.answer: No. Dictation can speed up typing, but you still need the facts, the times and the read-back in the record. Review every line before you save it or paste it into any system that holds patient data.

costs.title: A late or vague call
costs.text: When the call is late or unclear, the provider has to ask questions before deciding anything. The patient keeps going in the meantime. A call that sounds like a guess costs time on both ends, and a short, specific call is usually the fastest route to the right orders.

costs.title: Your own stress
costs.text: The NCSBN 2024 National Nursing Workforce Study reports 39.9% of RNs intend to leave or retire within five years. Among nurses planning to leave, excluding retirement, about 41.5% named stress and burnout as the root cause. Carrying a call you did not make can add to that load.

costs.title: A record that is hard to explain
costs.text: A call you skip, or one with no time and no response on record, is hard to explain later. Providers may also stop reading your calls as urgent if every call sounds routine. Both problems take time to repair, and both are avoidable with a short note.

costs.title: Rebuilding the call from memory
costs.text: Nurses without a script often rebuild the call in their heads while the patient waits. That mental load pulls focus from the rest of the assignment. A one-page card takes a few minutes to make and reduces the rebuilding each time you need it.

causes.title: Not knowing how to start
causes.text: Structured tools exist, but many nurses still hesitate before they call. In the escalation pathway study, 48 of 89 respondents who had faced a concern hesitated because they were not sure how to escalate. That is 53.9% of that group. Unclear steps can stop a call before it starts.

causes.title: The matrix is hard to use
causes.text: In the same study, 47% were still unsure how to use the escalation matrix. Another 41% were ambivalent about whether the pathway had improved their confidence. A chart that people cannot read quickly does not help during a busy night shift.

causes.title: Numbers are held back
causes.text: The full matrix with phone numbers was held by nursing managers, while posted copies omitted the numbers. On a night call, a nurse who sees a name but no number cannot act on it. The fix sits with whoever controls the copy.

causes.title: Contacts past the provider are unclear
causes.text: Staff knew the provider and the immediate supervisor. Contacts beyond those two were unclear. When the first call fails, that gap decides whether the patient gets a second call at all, so it matters more than it looks on a calm day.

causes.title: Fear of how the call will land
causes.text: Two respondents cited fear of retaliation. The count is small, and the response rate was about 9%, so it is not a prevalence figure. It still appears in nurses' own words, which makes it worth raising with your unit leaders in a calm conversation.

fixes.title: Build a one-page SBAR card
fixes.text: Keep S, B, A and R on one printed page, with a line for the read-back, the time, and the name of the person you reached. Make it in Word with Insert > Table and four rows. Put it where you start your shift, not in a drawer you open only when something goes wrong.

fixes.title: Get the numbers, then check the posted copy
fixes.text: Ask your manager for the full escalation matrix with phone numbers. Compare it with the posted copy. Where the posted copy is missing numbers, flag it, and write the numbers on your card in pencil so you can update them when they change.

fixes.title: Write the chain of command in order
fixes.text: Write the contacts in the order your policy says to use them. If the policy is unclear, ask your manager to confirm the order in writing. Then follow the chain as written, so you do not have to rebuild it at two in the morning from memory.

fixes.title: Say the call aloud on a quiet shift
fixes.text: Practice with a colleague if you can. Read the card aloud, one line for each part. Change any line that sounds like an apology or a question. A call is easier to make at night when you have already said it out loud once.

fixes.title: Ask for read-back, every time
fixes.text: Repeat each order back and ask the provider to confirm it. Write the order, the time and the name. This takes seconds and reduces the chance of a misheard order. Use the same habit for verbal orders, the way your policy describes.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Get the numbers
plan.text: Ask your manager for the full escalation matrix with phone numbers. Compare it with the posted copy and note what is missing. Do this at the start of a day shift, when the manager is easiest to reach.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Build the card
plan.text: Make a one-page SBAR card in Word with Insert > Table. Add four rows, a read-back line, and the chain of command in order. Print it, keep one copy at the station and one in your bag.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Practice out loud
plan.text: Read the card aloud on a quiet shift, with a colleague if you can. Rewrite any line that sounds like a question or an apology. Keep the wording in your own words, so it sounds like you on the phone.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set up your Mac
plan.text: If work alerts reach your Mac, open System Settings > Focus, select your Focus, click Allowed Apps, and turn on Time Sensitive Notifications. Then check Notifications settings for that app and test it on a quiet day.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review after a real call
plan.text: After your next escalation, write down what worked and what did not. Update the card. Ask your manager whether the posted matrix needs the same fix, and keep the card at the station.
